Summary: Circumcision is the sign of God's covenant with Abraham, performed on Jewish boys on the eighth day after birth.
JewishBackground: Commanded in Genesis 17, circumcision marks every male child of the covenant people. It is performed at a brit milah, a covenant ceremony, and remains a defining practice of Jewish identity to this day.
PointsToChrist: The apostles wrestled with what circumcision meant for Gentile believers, and the Jerusalem council decided Gentiles need not be circumcised. Paul then points to the deeper reality: true circumcision is of the heart, by the Spirit, a mark every believer in Christ carries.

Summary: The Day of Atonement was the one day each year when the high priest entered the Most Holy Place to make atonement for Israel's sins.
JewishBackground: On the 10th of Tishri, Israel fasted and the high priest, after sacrifices for himself and the people, entered the Holy of Holies with blood, then sent a goat bearing the people's sins into the wilderness. It was the most solemn day of the Jewish year.
PointsToChrist: The letter to the Hebrews reads this day as a shadow of Christ: he entered the true Holy Place once for all, not with the blood of goats but with his own blood, securing an eternal redemption that yearly sacrifices could only picture.

Summary: Tabernacles, or Sukkot, remembers Israel's forty years in the wilderness, when families lived in fragile booths and God sheltered them.
JewishBackground: For seven days, families eat and sometimes sleep in a sukkah, a booth roofed with branches, and wave the lulav of palm, willow, myrtle, and citron. In Second Temple times the feast included a water-pouring ceremony and great lamps lighting the Temple courts.
PointsToChrist: John places two of Jesus' great claims at this feast: during the water ceremony he cries out that whoever thirsts should come to him for living water, and he declares himself the light of the world. And John opens his Gospel saying the Word became flesh and tabernacled among us.

Summary: The Feast of Trumpets opens the autumn holy days with the sounding of the shofar, calling God's people to attention and repentance.
JewishBackground: On the first day of Tishri, trumpets are blown over a holy assembly and no regular work is done. In later Jewish tradition the day is Rosh Hashanah, the New Year, opening ten days of repentance leading to the Day of Atonement.
PointsToChrist: For Messianic readers, the trumpet blast also sounds the future: Paul writes that at the last trumpet the dead will be raised, and that the Lord himself will descend with the sound of God's trumpet. The shofar that wakes a people to repentance points to the day the King returns.

Summary: Firstfruits offered the first sheaf of the barley harvest to God, a sign that the whole harvest belonged to him and that more was coming.
JewishBackground: On the day after the Sabbath during Unleavened Bread, a priest waved the first sheaf of barley before the Lord. No one ate of the new harvest until this offering was made, making the firstfruits both a gift and a pledge of the full harvest to come.
PointsToChrist: Paul calls the risen Christ the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep: his resurrection is the first sheaf, guaranteeing the resurrection of all who belong to him. The feast's timing, in Passover week, matches the weekend of his death and resurrection.

Summary: Hanukkah, the Festival of Lights, celebrates the rededication of the Temple in 164 BC after its desecration, and God's provision of oil for the menorah.
JewishBackground: When Judah Maccabee's forces retook Jerusalem, they cleansed the Temple and relit the menorah. Tradition holds that one day's supply of consecrated oil burned for eight days, and the feast is kept for eight nights with the lighting of the hanukkiah, games, and gifts.
PointsToChrist: John's Gospel notes that Jesus himself was in Jerusalem for the Feast of Dedication, walking in the Temple courts. The feast of light points naturally to the one who called himself the light of the world, rededicating not a building of stone but his own people.

Summary: Hebrew is the language of the Old Testament, a tongue whose words carry layers of meaning that translation can only partly convey.
JewishBackground: Biblical Hebrew's root system lets single words branch into families of meaning: shalom means peace, wholeness, and welfare; hesed means steadfast love, mercy, and loyalty. Wordplay runs through the text, from Adam formed from adamah, the ground, to names that tell a person's story.
PointsToChrist: The New Testament preserves the Hebrew world even in Greek: Jesus is Yeshua, a name meaning salvation, and Matthew ties that name to his mission, for he will save his people from their sins. Reading the Old Testament with Hebrew ears lets the Messiah's story sound in its original key.
RelatedEvents: The Ten Commandments; Ezra Reads the Law

Summary: Isaiah 53 pictures a servant who is pierced for our transgressions, crushed for our iniquities, and led like a lamb to the slaughter — yet whose suffering brings healing.
JewishBackground: In mainstream Jewish tradition, the servant is commonly understood as Israel itself, or the righteous remnant suffering for the nations. The passage sits within Isaiah's servant songs, written to exiles longing for redemption.
PointsToChrist: Messianic readers hear the servant as the Messiah: despised and rejected, wounded for transgressions, silent before shearers, assigned a grave with the rich — every detail fulfilled in Jesus' crucifixion. Philip used this very chapter to lead an Ethiopian official to faith in Jesus.

Summary: The ancient Jewish wedding unfolded in stages: betrothal, a price paid, the groom preparing a room in his father's house, and a return at an unknown hour to claim his bride.
JewishBackground: Betrothal was legally binding, sealed with a price, after which the groom departed to prepare a place while the bride waited, kept ready. His return came with a shout and a trumpet, often at night, and the celebration lasted days. The pattern shaped how ordinary Jews understood covenant love.
PointsToChrist: Jesus borrowed this pattern for his own promises: he goes to prepare a place and will return to take his people to himself, at an hour no one knows, like a bridegroom coming for his bride. Paul calls marriage itself a mystery pointing to Christ and the church, and Revelation ends with the marriage supper of the Lamb. This is a Messianic reading of the customs, offered as illustration, not as a claim about what every Jewish wedding meant.
RelatedEvents: Jesus Turns Water into Wine at Cana

Summary: Kosher law governs what observant Jews eat and how food is prepared, marking out a life set apart by God's commands.
JewishBackground: Leviticus and Deuteronomy list clean and unclean animals, forbid blood and certain mixtures, and require humane slaughter and the separation of meat and dairy. Keeping kosher is both obedience and daily identity, a reminder at every meal that God's people are holy.
PointsToChrist: The New Testament records Peter's vision of unclean animals with the command not to call unclean what God has made clean — a vision chiefly about welcoming Gentiles into the people of God. Many Messianic Jews continue to keep kosher as a matter of identity and witness, not as a means of salvation.

Summary: The mezuzah is a small case fixed to the doorposts of a Jewish home, holding a parchment inscribed with the Shema.
JewishBackground: Deuteronomy commands God's words to be written on the doorposts of houses and gates. The parchment inside a mezuzah carries the Shema and the passage on teaching children, so that crossing a threshold becomes a reminder of the covenant.
PointsToChrist: For Messianic readers, the mezuzah's Word on the doorway echoes the Word who became flesh and dwelt among us — the one who stands at the door and knocks. The practice turns an ordinary doorway into a daily confession of whose house this is.

Summary: Micah promised that from Bethlehem, small among the clans of Judah, would come a ruler whose origins are from of old, from ancient days.
JewishBackground: Bethlehem was David's town, and the promise tied the coming ruler to David's line. When Herod asked where the Messiah was to be born, the chief priests and scribes answered from this very verse: in Bethlehem of Judea.
PointsToChrist: Matthew records Jesus' birth in Bethlehem as the fulfillment of Micah's words, and John records the debate it caused — some dismissed Jesus because they thought he came from Galilee, missing the Bethlehem birth. The small town's small promise carries the weight of eternity: a ruler from ancient days, born in time.

Summary: The mikveh is a ritual bath of living water used for purification, conversion, and preparation for holy moments.
JewishBackground: Immersion in a mikveh marks transitions: after impurity, before marriage, and at conversion to Judaism, when the convert emerges as a new person. The bath must hold gathered rainwater or a flowing source, and the whole body goes under.
PointsToChrist: John the Baptist's immersions in the Jordan drew on this world, and Christian baptism carries the same shape deeper: buried with Christ and raised to new life. The mikveh's picture of washing and new beginning is fulfilled in the baptism of believers into Jesus.

Summary: The Seder is the ordered Passover meal in which the story of the Exodus is retold, tasted, and passed to children.
JewishBackground: The Seder follows a set order of fifteen steps, including four cups of wine — traditionally linked to sanctification, deliverance, redemption, and praise — bitter herbs, unleavened bread, and the afikoman: the middle matzah, broken, hidden, and later ransomed back by the children.
PointsToChrist: Messianic readers see the Seder's symbols fulfilled at the Last Supper: Jesus took bread, broke it, and called it his body, and took the cup after supper, the cup of redemption, as the new covenant in his blood. The hidden afikoman, broken and brought back, pictures the buried and risen Messiah — a Messianic reading, not the mainstream Jewish understanding of the custom.

Summary: Passover remembers the night God delivered Israel from slavery in Egypt, when the blood of a lamb on the doorposts spared the firstborn and Pharaoh finally let the people go.
JewishBackground: Passover is kept on the 14th of Nisan with a Seder meal: unleavened bread, bitter herbs, and the retelling of the Exodus. The seven-day Feast of Unleavened Bread follows immediately, remembering the haste of departure, when there was no time for bread to rise.
PointsToChrist: The New Testament presents Jesus as our Passover: John the Baptist calls him the Lamb of God, Paul writes that Christ our Passover lamb has been sacrificed, and the Last Supper takes place within a Passover meal, where the bread and cup are given new meaning.

Summary: The Pharisees were teachers of the law who shaped popular Judaism through study, synagogue teaching, and an oral tradition alongside the written Torah.
JewishBackground: Pharisees believed in resurrection, angels, and divine providence, and they brought Torah into daily life through detailed application. They were the most influential teachers of ordinary Jews, and their debates with Jesus fill the Gospels.
PointsToChrist: The Pharisees must not be caricatured: Nicodemus sought Jesus by night and defended him, Gamaliel urged restraint toward the apostles, and Paul proudly called himself a Pharisee. Jesus debated them fiercely precisely because they were serious about God — and because he claimed an authority greater than their tradition.

Summary: Psalm 22 opens with a cry of abandonment and moves, verse by verse, through suffering that ends in praise and a kingdom proclaimed to future generations.
JewishBackground: David's psalm describes mockery, pierced hands and feet, garments divided by lot, and bones out of joint — suffering that David knew, yet described in terms that reach beyond his own life. Jewish tradition reads it as David's prayer, and later as the voice of Israel in exile.
PointsToChrist: On the cross, Jesus quoted its first line, and the Gospel writers let its details tell the story: the mockery, the lots cast for his clothing, the thirst. The psalm does not end at the cross — it ends with all the ends of the earth turning to the Lord, which is exactly where the Gospel goes.

Summary: Purim celebrates the deliverance of the Jews of Persia from Haman's plot to destroy them, as told in the Book of Esther.
JewishBackground: On the 14th of Adar, Jews read the Megillah, the scroll of Esther, aloud, feast, give gifts of food, and give to the poor. Notably, God's name never appears in Esther — yet his providence is everywhere in the story's reversals.
PointsToChrist: Purim's hidden God who overturns gallows and thrones points to the same providence that preserved the people from whom the Messiah would come. The feast reminds believers that God is at work even when he is not named, and that deliverance often arrives through unlikely hands.

Summary: The Sadducees were the priestly aristocracy of the Second Temple, guardians of the Temple and its sacrifices.
JewishBackground: Drawn largely from wealthy priestly families, Sadducees held authority in the Temple and the Sanhedrin. They accepted only the written Torah, denied the resurrection, angels, and spirits, and were skeptical of the oral tradition the Pharisees prized.
PointsToChrist: The Sadducees questioned Jesus with a riddle about resurrection, and he answered from the Torah itself: God is the God of the living. Their power faded with the Temple's destruction in AD 70, but their question remains the question at the heart of the Gospel — is there life beyond death, and has God answered it?

Summary: Second Temple Judaism is the world of Jesus: Jewish life from the rebuilding of the Temple after exile until its destruction by Rome in AD 70.
JewishBackground: After the exile, Jewish life reorganized around Torah, synagogue, and Temple, while living under Persian, Greek, and Roman rule. Sects formed — Pharisees, Sadducees, Essenes, Zealots — and expectation of a Messiah ran high, shaped by prophets and by suffering under foreign powers.
PointsToChrist: The Gospels cannot be understood apart from this world: its festivals set Jesus' calendar, its synagogues hosted his teaching, its Temple framed his death, and its Messianic hopes explain both the crowds that hailed him and the leaders who rejected him. He came, Paul writes, in the fullness of time.
RelatedEvents: Rebuilding of the Temple; The Crucifixion

Summary: Shabbat, the Sabbath, is the weekly day of rest commanded from Creation itself, a holy pause from work for worship, family, and delight in God.
JewishBackground: From Friday sunset to Saturday sunset, observant Jews cease creative work, light candles, bless bread and wine, share festive meals, and gather for prayer and Torah study. The Sabbath remembers both Creation and the Exodus: God rested, and God freed slaves who could not rest.
PointsToChrist: Jesus called himself Lord of the Sabbath and taught that the Sabbath was made for people, not people for the Sabbath. Hebrews then holds out a deeper rest: the Sabbath rest that remains for God's people is found in Christ, in whom striving ceases.

Summary: Shavuot, the Feast of Weeks, falls fifty days after Firstfruits and celebrates the wheat harvest — and, by tradition, the giving of the Torah at Mount Sinai.
JewishBackground: Shavuot is one of the three pilgrimage feasts, when Israelites brought two loaves of wheat bread to the Temple. Later Jewish tradition ties the day to Sinai and reads the Book of Ruth in the synagogue.
PointsToChrist: On Shavuot the Holy Spirit fell on the first believers in Jerusalem, and about three thousand were added to the church in one day. What began at Sinai with law written on stone continued at Pentecost with the Spirit writing on hearts.

Summary: The synagogue is the local house of prayer, study, and assembly that became the center of Jewish life after the exile.
JewishBackground: With no sacrifices offered there, the synagogue's life centers on prayer, the reading of Torah and Prophets, teaching, and community. By Jesus' day, synagogues stood in towns across the land, and visiting teachers were invited to read and speak.
PointsToChrist: Jesus' own ministry moved through synagogues: he taught in them, read Isaiah in Nazareth's synagogue and announced its fulfillment, and his followers carried the same pattern to synagogues across the Roman world, where the message of the Messiah was first preached.

Summary: The Temple in Jerusalem was the place of God's dwelling, where priests offered daily sacrifices for atonement, thanksgiving, and fellowship.
JewishBackground: From the tabernacle to Solomon's Temple and the Second Temple, Israel's worship centered on sacrifice: burnt offerings, grain offerings, peace offerings, sin offerings, and guilt offerings, with the high priest mediating on the Day of Atonement. The Temple was destroyed by Rome in AD 70.
PointsToChrist: Jesus called his own body the temple and presented himself as the final sacrifice: the Lamb who takes away sin, the great high priest who mediates a new covenant. With his death, the sacrificial system found its completion, and his people became the temple of the living God.
RelatedEvents: Building of Solomon's Temple; The Crucifixion

Summary: The menorah is the seven-branched golden lampstand that burned continually in the tabernacle and the Temple.
JewishBackground: Crafted from a single talent of pure gold with almond-blossom cups, the menorah's seven lamps were tended daily by the priests and burned from evening to morning. Its light symbolized God's presence and Israel's calling to be a light to the nations.
PointsToChrist: Jesus declared himself the light of the world, and Revelation pictures the risen Christ standing among seven golden lampstands, the churches. The Temple lamp that never went out points to the one whose light darkness cannot overcome.

Summary: The Passover lamb was unblemished, slain at twilight, its blood marking the doorposts of every house that would be spared.
JewishBackground: Exodus commands a lamb without defect, kept from the tenth day and slain on the fourteenth, with none of its bones broken, its blood painted on the lintel and doorposts. The lamb's death stood between Israel and judgment, and its flesh fed the people on their journey out.
PointsToChrist: John the Baptist pointed at Jesus and said, Behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world. John notes that Jesus' legs were not broken on the cross, like the Passover lamb's bones, and Paul states it plainly: Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed.

Summary: On the Day of Atonement, two goats stood before the Lord: one sacrificed, one sent alive into the wilderness bearing the sins of the people.
JewishBackground: The high priest laid both hands on the live goat, confessed over it all the iniquities of Israel, and sent it away by a fit man into the wilderness, carrying sins to a land that is not inhabited. The two goats together pictured atonement: death for sin, and sin carried away.
PointsToChrist: Messianic readers see both goats fulfilled in Jesus: he died as the sacrifice for sin, and he carried our sins away — outside the camp, as Hebrews puts it, bearing our shame. The scapegoat's journey into the wilderness is the picture of sins remembered no more.

Summary: The Shema is Judaism's central confession, recited morning and evening: Hear, O Israel, the Lord our God, the Lord is one.
JewishBackground: Deuteronomy 6:4-9 commands Israel to love God with heart, soul, and strength, to teach these words to children, and to bind them on hand and forehead and write them on doorposts. The Shema anchors Jewish prayer and identity, confessing one God and one covenant.
PointsToChrist: Jesus himself affirmed the Shema as the first and greatest commandment. Mainstream Jewish tradition holds God's oneness in a way that excludes the Trinity, while Messianic readers confess the same one God, revealed in the Messiah Jesus. The difference is stated here plainly, not as a point of mockery: the Shema is holy ground for both.

Summary: The Torah, the five books of Moses, is the foundation of the Hebrew Bible and the story of God's covenant from Creation to the edge of the Promised Land.
JewishBackground: Torah means instruction, not merely law. Genesis through Deuteronomy carry Creation, the patriarchs, the Exodus, Sinai, and the wilderness, and are read aloud in synagogue in an annual cycle, portion by portion, so that the whole community hears the whole story every year.
PointsToChrist: Jesus said he came not to abolish the Torah but to fulfill it, and on the road to Emmaus he showed how Moses and all the Prophets spoke of him. For Messianic readers, the Torah is not a ladder to climb to God but a signpost pointing to the one who climbed down to us.
RelatedEvents: The Ten Commandments; Ezra Reads the Law

Summary: Zechariah promises a day when God will pour out grace and the people will look on the one they have pierced, and mourn for him as for an only child.
JewishBackground: Spoken to Jerusalem in a prophecy of siege and deliverance, the verse pictures a pierced figure whose wounding brings national repentance. Jewish readings of the pierced one have varied across the centuries, and the passage remains one of the most discussed in the prophets.
PointsToChrist: The New Testament applies the verse directly to Jesus: John records the soldier piercing his side and cites Zechariah, and Revelation pictures every eye seeing him, even those who pierced him. For Messianic readers, the mourning Zechariah foresaw begins at the cross and continues until the day of his return.
